TRADE SECRET PREEMPTION DOCTRINE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS TRADE SECRET PREEMPTION DOCTRINE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's trade secret preemption doctrine under Civil Code section 3426.7, part of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA) — the statutory provision that addresses which other civil claims may, and may not, be brought alongside or instead of a trade secret misappropriation claim when those claims rest on the same underlying facts. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning a situation involving Acme, Inc. and Beta Corp. The other claims or remedies under consideration, beyond a trade secret misappropriation claim itself, are described as follows: Breach of contract, breach of confidence, unfair competition. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what section 3426.7 says and how published California case law has construed it. It does not itself determine whether any specific claim described above is, or is not, based on the same nucleus of facts as a trade secret misappropriation claim, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and is meant as a companion to, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter document: that document addresses the definition of misappropriation and the remedies available for it, while this one addresses a separate question — what happens to other, non-trade-secret civil claims arising from the same facts.

WHAT CUTSA DOES NOT SUPERSEDE: OTHER TRADE-SECRET-SPECIFIC STATUTES
California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act is not, by its own terms, a complete replacement for every other California statute that touches trade secrets. Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (a), states that unless a statute expressly provides otherwise, CUTSA does not supersede any other statute relating to trade secret misappropriation or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets. This subdivision addresses CUTSA's relationship to other trade-secret-specific statutes; it is a separate question from subdivision (b) of the same section, addressed in a companion clause of this document, which addresses CUTSA's relationship to non-statutory common-law claims and other civil, contractual, and criminal remedies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Except as otherwise expressly provided, this title does not supersede any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret, or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(a) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other trade-secret-specific statutes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.7.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of CUTSA's own stated relationship to other trade-secret-specific statutes — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not an exhaustive list of which other California statutes "relat[e] to misappropriation of a trade secret" or "otherwise regulat[e] trade secrets" for purposes of this subdivision; no such statute is identified or discussed here. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of Cal. Civ. Code section 3426.7; a companion clause in this document quotes subdivision (b) and another quotes subdivision (c) of that same section — all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other, and are disclosed as such throughout this document. The full text of section 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov — the official California Legislative Information website — as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section (after whitespace normalization), so this is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. No case law construing subdivision (a) specifically was checked in this research; the subdivision's own text is unambiguous on its face, so the statute stands as the source here without a corroborating case. This is California-specific: CUTSA preemption doctrine, including this non-supersession rule, is a creature of California statute, and many other states have adopted their own versions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act with their own (not necessarily identical) provisions on this same question, which this document does not address.

WHAT CUTSA DOES NOT AFFECT: CONTRACTUAL, CRIMINAL, AND NON-TRADE-SECRET CIVIL REMEDIES
Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (b), expressly preserves three categories of remedy from CUTSA's displacing effect: (1) contractual remedies, whether or not they are also based on trade secret misappropriation; (2) other civil remedies that are not based on trade secret misappropriation; and (3) criminal remedies, whether or not they are also based on trade secret misappropriation. This is the core statutory text underlying what courts and litigants commonly call "CUTSA preemption" — a claim falling within one of these three preserved categories is not displaced by CUTSA merely because the same underlying facts could also support a trade secret misappropriation claim. Notably, the statutory text of section 3426.7 does not itself use the word "preempt" or "preemption" anywhere; that terminology comes from courts construing this subdivision, not from the statute's own language, as described in a companion clause of this document.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]

  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.7.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of what CUTSA expressly preserves — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific claim described in this Information Sheet falls into one of these three preserved categories; that is a fact-specific characterization this document does not make. The full text of section 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section (after whitespace normalization), so this is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. This document's own text-search of both retrieved copies of section 3426.7 confirmed that neither the word "preempt" nor "preemption" (nor any variant) appears anywhere in the statute's text; the statute instead uses "supersede" (in subdivision (a)) and "does not affect" (in subdivision (b) and (c)). This is California-specific: many other states have adopted their own versions of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, several with their own preemption or displacement provisions that are not necessarily worded or construed identically to California's, and this document does not address them.

A SEPARATE CARVE-OUT: THE CALIFORNIA PUBLIC RECORDS ACT
Civil Code section 3426.7, subdivision (c), sets out a further, narrower carve-out specific to public records: CUTSA does not affect the disclosure of a record by a state or local agency under the California Public Records Act. The statute directs that whether disclosure of a record under the Public Records Act would constitute a trade secret misappropriation, and what rights and remedies would apply, is instead governed by the law that was in effect before CUTSA's own operative date. This is a distinct, narrower preservation than the general categories described in subdivision (b) — it addresses only agency records-disclosure questions, not the broader universe of contractual, criminal, and non-trade-secret civil claims.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "This title does not affect the disclosure of a record by a state or local agency under the California Public Records Act (Division 10 (commencing with Section 7920.000) of Title 1 of the Government Code). Any determination as to whether the disclosure of a record under the California Public Records Act constitutes a misappropriation of a trade secret and the rights and remedies with respect thereto shall be made pursuant to the law in effect before the operative date of this title."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on Public Records Act disclosures (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.7.)
  Known gap: This is California's statute, used as real evidence of a specific, additional carve-out in CUTSA's displacement provision — not a claim about which jurisdiction's law governs any specific dispute, and not an explanation of what "the law in effect before the operative date of this title" actually required; that pre-CUTSA law is not researched or described anywhere in this document. Code section 3426.7; companion clauses in this document quote subdivisions (a) and (b) of that same section — all three are subdivisions of one statutory section, not independent sources of each other. The full text of section 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical text for the whole section (after whitespace normalization), so this is one primary source checked twice for consistency, not two independent sources. No case law construing subdivision (c) specifically was checked in this research. This is California-specific: the California Public Records Act itself, and this carve-out's interaction with it, are matters of California law only, and this document does not address how any other state's public-records or trade-secret statute would treat the same question.

CASE LAW: THE "SAME NUCLEUS OF FACTS" TEST FOR CUTSA PREEMPTION
Although section 3426.7's own text never uses the word "preempt" or "preemption," published California case law construing that section does use that terminology, and has developed a specific test for applying it. In K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., the California Court of Appeal held that section 3426.7, subdivision (b), preempts common-law claims that are based on the same nucleus of facts as a trade secret misappropriation claim — adopting, as California law, a test the court found in earlier federal decisions applying California law. Under this test, whether a particular non-trade-secret civil claim survives alongside a trade secret misappropriation claim can turn on whether that claim rests on facts distinct from the misappropriation, or instead restates the same underlying factual allegations under a different legal label.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "In sum, we agree with the federal cases applying California law, which hold that section 3426.7, subdivision (b), preempts common law claims that are “based on the same nucleus of facts as the misappropriation of trade secrets claim for relief.”"
  — K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal. App. 4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist., Mar. 3, 2009), California Court of Appeal, Sixth Appellate District, adopting the "same nucleus of facts" test for CUTSA preemption (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256761/kc-multimedia-inc-v-bank-of-america-technology-operations-inc/)

App., 6th Dist. 2009), is a published opinion of the California Court of Appeal, confirmed as "Published" status via the CourtListener database. Its text was retrieved via CourtListener's document-read function (returning the opinion's full html-with-citations text) and the exact quoted sentence was independently re-confirmed as an exact match via a separate CourtListener full-text search query for that phrase — both checks queried the same underlying CourtListener database rather than two independently published sources, so this is one primary source (the published opinion) checked two different ways, not two independent sources, and is disclosed on that basis. The same phrase, and citation to this case, also appeared in results from other, later opinions in that same search (for example, a 2014 federal district court decision applying California law), which were not independently read or verified in this research and are not cited here; they are mentioned only to note that this test has been repeated elsewhere, not as an independently verified additional source. This is a single California Court of Appeal decision from one appellate district (the Sixth Appellate District); it is not a California Supreme Court decision, and this document does not represent that every California appellate district has adopted identical language for this test, or that no California case has stated the test differently. This is California-specific case law construing a California statute; it says nothing about how any other state's version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act treats the same question.

CASE LAW: HOW THE TEST WAS APPLIED TO SPECIFIC COMMON-LAW CLAIMS
In the same decision, the California Court of Appeal applied the "same nucleus of facts" test to the specific claims pleaded in that case and affirmed the trial court's conclusion that the plaintiff's claims for breach of confidence, interference with contract, and statutory unfair competition were all preempted by CUTSA, because each rested on the same factual allegations as the plaintiff's trade secret misappropriation claim. This illustrates that the same test can reach claims styled under a range of different common-law and statutory labels — the label a claim is given does not by itself determine whether it survives; the test instead looks to whether the claim's factual basis is the same as, or distinct from, the trade secret misappropriation claim's factual basis.

Applying that construction to the operative pleading here, we agree with the trial court’s conclusion that appellant’s claims for breach of confidence, interference with contract, and statutory unfair competition are all preempted by CUTSA."
  — K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal. App. 4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist., Mar. 3, 2009), California Court of Appeal, Sixth Appellate District, application of CUTSA preemption to breach of confidence, interference with contract, and unfair competition claims (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256761/kc-multimedia-inc-v-bank-of-america-technology-operations-inc/)
  Known gap: This is the same K.C. Multimedia, Inc. v. Bank of America Technology & Operations, Inc., 171 Cal.App.4th 939 (Cal. Ct. App., 6th Dist. 2009) opinion quoted in the companion case-law clause of this document — not an independent source from it, and disclosed as such. This clause quotes a different passage of that same opinion (the court's application of the test to the specific claims before it, near the end of its preemption discussion), rather than the passage stating the test itself; the two passages are treated here as one source, not independently corroborating ones. This clause describes what claims were found preempted on the specific pleading before that court; it does not state that breach of confidence, interference with contract, or unfair competition claims are always, or even usually, preempted — the same test applied to a differently pleaded claim, resting on facts distinct from the misappropriation itself, can reach the opposite result, and this document does not evaluate that question for any specific claim. This is a single published California Court of Appeal decision from one appellate district; it is not a California Supreme Court decision. This is California-specific case law construing a California statute; it says nothing about how any other state's version of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act, or that state's own preemption case law, would treat the same or similarly labeled claims.
